strengths: Addresses an important question: what multimodal contrastive learning recovers when modalities have distinct generators and imperfectly shared latent factors.

The proposed CLIP postprocessing is simple and potentially useful. Table 2 reports improvements for ViT-B/16 from 44.97% to 46.57% on 2-shot ImageNet and from 32.51% to 37.13% averaged across target distributions.
The evaluation spans synthetic assumption violations, four CLIP backbones, multiple shot counts, 11 adaptation datasets, CelebA traversals, and ground-truth latent recovery on Multimodal3DIdent.
weaknesses: The central proofs depend on a false lemma. Lemma 2 in Appendix D.1 asserts that the minimum normalized contrastive loss is zero. Under Eq. (4), with matched temperature, the latent identity encoders instead achieve −2I(z_x;z_t)<0. Moreover, its condition C1 requires identical embeddings almost surely for noisy positive pairs. Under the full-support vMF coupling with independent nuisances, this forces constant embeddings, contradicting C2's uniformity requirement. Consequently, the shared, nuisance-free mapping used to establish both identifiability results is not justified.

The convex-body argument has additional substantive problems. Lemma 3 establishes uniformity of p(z_t) only in the limit λ→0, but Eq. (43) uses exact uniformity to prove a theorem stated for finite λ. A uniform variable on [0,1] followed by a truncated Laplace conditional generally produces a nonuniform marginal. Furthermore, Corollary 2 omits the appendix's essential restriction to Lp geometry with p≠2; Euclidean balls admit arbitrary rotations, contradicting permutation-only identifiability.

The claimed ICA disentanglement guarantee is incompatible with the spherical assumptions. Uniform spherical coordinates are dependent, and their distribution is invariant under every orthogonal transformation, leaving no identifiable orientation for FastICA to recover. Having M−1 degrees of freedom does not establish independent linear sources. The proposed local-isometry/PCA argument is also heuristic and does not establish recovery guarantees for normalized CLIP representations.

The downstream experiments do not isolate disentanglement as the source of improvement. FastICA includes whitening and dimensionality reduction, while the compared pipelines use different component counts. Matched PCA-only and whitening baselines are missing. Since L2-regularized linear classification is invariant to an orthogonal feature rotation, conditioning and dimensionality reduction provide alternative explanations for the gains.

The recovery evaluation is weaker than the claims. Appendix K regresses learned representations on ground-truth factors; this can yield R²=1 for a rank-deficient projection that loses latent information. Recovering ground-truth factors from representations and checking invertibility would be more appropriate. Appendix P's aggregate R² and selected CelebA traversals also do not establish component-wise disentanglement.

The experimental reporting leaves material uncertainty. PCA/ICA fitting splits and component-selection procedures are insufficiently specified, the real-data accuracy tables lack uncertainty estimates, and the Multimodal3DIdent training protocol is underdescribed. Table 2 also reports the RN101 baseline target average as 20.03%, although its four entries average approximately 22.03%, overstating the corresponding improvement.

The 'beyond DAGs' contribution is insufficiently established. An undirected statistical dependence does not itself demonstrate greater explanatory power than latent-confounder or regime-mixture DAG formulations. The experiments do not directly test the heterogeneous, opposing causal mechanisms motivating the model, and much of the subsequent identifiability machinery is inherited from Zimmermann et al. (2021).
